# Gunpowder (black powder) (`gunpowder`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: needs saltpetre_production
- Core idea: Black powder originated in China. Saltpetre acts as an oxidiser, allowing the fuel to burn rapidly even in confinement. Burning produces gases and solid residues, which account for both its propulsive effect and its conspicuous smoke. Chinese sources document incendiaries before bombs and guns. Later European powder mills developed corned powder, which was easier to transport consistently than loose meal powder. Access to saltpetre, skilled mill workers and reliable state supplies shaped the spread of firearms. Fire and explosion were persistent hazards throughout the industry.
- Pitfalls:
  - Taking one modern composition as typical of all historical powders. Early Chinese texts describe materials with different purposes.
  - Treating corning as the invention of gunpowder. It altered the physical form of an existing material.
  - Assuming a state that knew of gunpowder could supply it in quantity. Access to saltpetre, transport and specialised mills mattered.
  - Believing that the Chinese used powder only for fireworks. Chinese armies employed incendiaries, bombs, rockets and guns.
- History: china: c. 850 – Daoist text warns that saltpetre, sulphur and honey burn violently; 1044 – Wujing Zongyao gives the first written formulas (low-nitrate incendiaries); 13th c. – explosive high-nitrate powder and iron bombs; islamic: c. 1240 – Ibn al-Baytar calls saltpetre 'snow of China'; c. 1280 – Hasan al-Rammah gives recipes and the purification of saltpetre with wood ash; india: 13th–14th c. – arrives, probably with the Mongols; widespread in the 15th c.; east_asia: 1377 – Korean powder office founded on the initiative of Choe Mu-seon; europe: c. 1267 – Roger Bacon describes firecrackers (the famous coded formula attributed to him is doubtful); c. 1300 – recipes in the Liber ignium; c. 1400–1430 – corned powder
- Read:
  - Joseph Needham et al., Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 part 7: Military Technology: The Gunpowder Epic (1986)
  - J. R. Partington, A History of Greek Fire and Gunpowder (1960)
  - Tonio Andrade, The Gunpowder Age (2016)
